To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the strategic process of universities is a complex process, which can be fruitfully analysed using the tools of the real options approach to strategy formation and implementation.

universities need to understand their own strategic processes better, and that the best way of achieving this understanding is through the application of real options theory to universities' strategies and strategic processes.

(1) universities' strategies are not the product of a formal planning process but of a complex, path-dependent process of strategic learning; (2) universities' strategies should not be seen as the result of a formal planning exercise, but as the result of an iterative, path-dependent process, which can be understood through the framework of real options analysis; and (3) universities should not attempt to plan, but should attempt to manage their strategic options.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the development of a new approach to strategy in universities, which is based on a more realistic view of the nature and process of strategy, and which is more consistent with the nature of universities as organizations.

the nature of strategy in the context of the complex and dynamic systems of universities, and with the implications for the development of strategy in universities of the insights of the real options approach.
developing a new approach to the understanding of universities' strategy, based on the development of a real options framework for the analysis of universities' strategic processes.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
universities should adopt a strategy model that is based on the concept of real options.
the strategic process of universities is best seen as a process of real option analysis, in the context of the complex and path-dependent nature of universities as ‘loose-couple’ organizations.
the private and public sector models for strategies in universities are very different from one another, and that there is a great deal of room for the development and application of the latter.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

universities' strategy is best seen as a real option process, which is not only path-dependent but which also involves a high degree of ‘looseness’ or ‘coupling’ in the way in which it is put into practice.
we have been concerned to develop a framework for understanding and managing strategic change in universities.
the strategic process of universities can be usefully understood through real options analysis.
The main takeaway from our work is that
universities should not be expected to be like commercial enterprises, but that they can be expected to be more like them than they have been.

universities' strategy formation and implementation processes can usefully be seen through the lenses of real options analysis, in a way that can accommodate both the complexity of universities' strategic process and the rich traditions and practices of the sector.
the private sector model is not a good model for the public sector model.
